shots.phrase: Begin by framing The Disciplined Solution Framework as a question about inputs, decisions, and observable results.

Consider this worked case: Sorting an array: Input is an unordered list of numbers; Output is the same list in non-decreasing order; Correctness is proved by loop invariants; Complexity is O(n log n) via divide-and-conquer.
List the givens before choosing a method, because an unstated assumption can change the conclusion.
Now define Asymptotic Notation and Growth precisely enough that another learner could test the definition.
Consider this worked case: If an algorithm performs 5n + 3 operations, its asymptotic growth is Θ(n), meaning it scales linearly with input size.
Separate the formal definition from an implementation detail, then identify what evidence would distinguish them.
With the foundation in place, examine how Loop Invariants for Correctness operates in a concrete sequence.

Consider this worked case: In bubble sort, the invariant 'the first i elements are sorted' holds before the loop (i=0), is maintained by swapping adjacent out-of-order elements, and guarantees the whole array is sorted when i=n.
Follow every arrow in order and name the state before and after each transition.
Next, compare the choices involved in Divide-and-Conquer Strategy and make the decision criteria explicit.
Consider this worked case: Merge sort divides an array into two halves, recursively sorts each half, then merges the two sorted halves in linear time.
Compare alternatives against the same constraints so the evaluation does not move the goalposts.
Apply Recurrences and Their Solutions to a worked situation instead of treating it as an isolated definition.
Consider this worked case: The recurrence T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n for merge sort solves to T(n) = Θ(n log n) via the Master Theorem.
Work from the concrete inputs to the result, checking units, types, or invariants at each step.
Examine the tradeoffs in Core Data Structures: Lists, Stacks, Queues, including what improves and what becomes more difficult.
Consider this worked case: A stack of plates: the last plate placed is the first one removed; a queue of customers: the first person in line is served first.
State the benefit, the cost, and the condition under which the tradeoff is acceptable.
Stress-test the reasoning around Trees and Hierarchical Representation with an edge case and identify which assumption controls the outcome.
Consider this worked case: A binary search tree stores keys so that left children are smaller and right children are larger, enabling O(log n) search on balanced trees.
Change one assumption at a time and observe which part of the reasoning no longer holds.
Use Hash Tables and Collision Strategies to diagnose a failure by separating symptoms, causes, and corrective action.
Consider this worked case: With hash function h(k) = k mod 7, keys 10 and 17 both map to index 3; chaining stores both in a linked list at that index.
Locate the first point where observed behavior diverges from expected behavior, then test the smallest plausible cause.
Connect Graph Representations and Traversal to the earlier ideas and explain how the pieces work as one system.
Consider this worked case: In a directed graph, a depth-first search (DFS) explores all reachable vertices from a start node, useful for topological ordering.
Explain each connection explicitly and verify that information retains the same meaning across representations.
Finish with Practical Analysis Checklist as a practical checklist that can guide a new analysis.

Consider this worked case: For Dijkstra's shortest path: define input as weighted graph and output as distance array; prove correctness via loop invariant that visited nodes have optimal distances; analyze time as O((V+E) log V).
For each checklist item, record the evidence, the remaining uncertainty, and the next verification step.
